lessons.title: Principles of Potato Storage
lessons.body:
Potatoes are living tubers that continue to breathe and lose moisture after harvest. To store them well, you must slow down this breathing without killing the tuber. The goal is to keep potatoes firm, sprout-free, and disease-free for as long as possible. The three key factors are temperature, humidity, and ventilation. For table potatoes, aim for 4â7Â°C and 90â95% relative humidity. For processing potatoes (chips and fries), store at 7â10Â°C to avoid too much sugar buildup. Never store potatoes in direct sunlight or in hot roomsâthey turn green and produce solanine, which is toxic.

Before storage, potatoes need to cure. Curing heals cuts and thickens the skin. Spread potatoes in a shaded, well-ventilated area at 15â20Â°C and 85â90% humidity for 10â14 days. This reduces weight loss and rot. After curing, gradually lower the temperature to the target storage range over 2â3 weeks. Sudden temperature drops can cause black spot or sweetening.

Sort potatoes before storage. Remove any with cuts, bruises, or signs of disease. One rotten potato can spoil many others. Store only healthy, mature tubers. In Africa, many farmers use traditional stores like pits, clamps, or raised cribs. These work if kept dry and ventilated. For small quantities, use jute sacks in a dark, cool room. Never use airtight plastic bagsâthey trap moisture and cause rot.

Regular inspection is critical. Check stored potatoes every two weeks. Remove sprouts, soft spots, or mouldy tubers immediately. Keep rodents and insects out. With good practices, table potatoes can store for 3â6 months, and processing potatoes for 4â8 months. Proper storage means less waste and more income.

lessons.title: Storage Facility Design and Ventilation
lessons.body:
A good storage facility protects potatoes from heat, cold, rain, and pests while allowing air to move. In Africa, you can build a simple but effective store using locally available materials. The basic design is a raised, slatted structure with a roof. The floor should be at least 30 cm above ground to prevent moisture and rodents. Use wooden slats spaced 2â3 cm apart for walls and floor so air can pass through. Cover the roof with grass thatch, iron sheets, or tarpaulin to block sun and rain. Leave openings at the bottom and top for ventilation. A store of 2 m x 3 m x 2 m can hold about 1,000 kg of potatoes.

Ventilation is the key to preventing heat and moisture buildup. Hot air rises and escapes through top vents, pulling fresh air in from bottom vents. This natural convection works well if the store is not too wide. For larger stores, you may need a small fan. In humid areas, use a dehumidifier or increase ventilation. Never block vents with sacks or debris. Air must flow around every potato. Stack potatoes no more than 1.5 m high to avoid crushing and to allow air circulation. Use crates or mesh bags instead of piling loose.

For bulk storage, consider a forced-air system. A small fan (50â100 W) connected to a duct under the pile can push air through. This is useful for curing and cooling. If you cannot afford a fan, rely on passive ventilation and keep the store shaded. In very hot regions, dig a pit store 1 m deep, line it with straw, and cover with a ventilated lid. Pit stores keep potatoes cool but must be kept dry.

Always monitor temperature and humidity. Hang a thermometer and hygrometer inside the store. If temperature rises above 10Â°C for table potatoes, increase ventilation. If humidity drops below 85%, sprinkle water on the floor (not on potatoes). With good design, you can store potatoes for months with minimal loss.

lessons.title: Managing Temperature and Humidity
lessons.body:
Temperature and humidity control is the difference between a good harvest and a rotten one. Potatoes are 80% water, so they lose weight and quality if humidity is too low. If humidity is too high, mould and bacteria grow. The ideal range is 90â95% relative humidity for table potatoes and 95â98% for processing potatoes. You can measure humidity with a hygrometer (costs about $10â20). If you don't have one, watch for signs: potatoes shrink and feel soft when humidity is low; they feel wet and develop mould when humidity is high.

Temperature control starts at harvest. After curing, lower the temperature slowly. For every 1Â°C drop, potatoes produce less heat and breathe slower. But do not go below 4Â°C for table potatoesâthat causes chilling injury and sweetening. For processing potatoes, keep at 7â10Â°C to avoid sugar accumulation that makes fries dark. In hot African climates, you may need a cool store. A simple evaporative cooler (charcoal cooler) can lower temperature by 5â10Â°C. Build a double-walled box with wet sand or charcoal between walls. Air passing through the wet layer cools down. This works well in dry areas.

Monitor temperature daily. Use a max-min thermometer. If temperature rises, increase ventilation. If it falls too low, close vents or add insulation. In cold highland areas, potatoes can freeze if stored below 0Â°C. Insulate with straw or move potatoes to a warmer room.

Humidity control: If too dry, place shallow pans of water on the floor or wet the floor. If too wet, increase ventilation and reduce the amount of potatoes per room. Never sprinkle water directly on potatoesâthat invites rot. For small quantities, store potatoes in perforated plastic bags or jute sacks. Jute breathes and helps regulate humidity. Check stored potatoes weekly. Remove any that are soft, sprouting, or mouldy. With careful management, you can keep potatoes fresh for 4â6 months.

lessons.title: Disease and Pest Control in Storage
lessons.body:
Even healthy-looking potatoes can carry hidden diseases. The most common storage diseases are late blight, dry rot, soft rot, and black scurf. Late blight causes brown, greasy patches and a foul smell. Dry rot creates sunken, wrinkled spots with white or pink mould. Soft rot turns potatoes into a smelly, wet mass. Black scurf leaves black spots on the skin. These diseases spread fast in warm, humid conditions. The best control is prevention: store only clean, undamaged potatoes; cure properly; keep temperature and humidity in the right range; and remove infected tubers immediately.

Pests in storage include potato tuber moth, rats, mice, and ants. Tuber moth larvae tunnel into potatoes, leaving frass (sawdust-like waste). To control moths, use pheromone traps or store potatoes in mesh bags with neem leaves. Neem leaves repel insects. For rats and mice, keep the store clean, seal cracks, and use traps or cats. Avoid poisons that can contaminate potatoes. Ants can be deterred by placing ashes or diatomaceous earth around the store.

Good hygiene is your best defence. Before storing a new crop, clean the store thoroughly. Remove all old potatoes, dust, and debris. Wash walls and floor with a disinfectant (e.g., bleach solution: 1 part bleach to 10 parts water). Let it dry completely. Use clean crates or bags. Never mix old and new potatoes. Inspect stored potatoes every two weeks. Wear gloves and remove any rotten, sprouting, or diseased tubers. Put them in a sealed bag and dispose of them away from the store. Do not compost diseased potatoesâburn or bury them deep.

If you see signs of disease, lower temperature to 4Â°C (for table potatoes) to slow spread. Improve ventilation to reduce moisture. For tuber moth, you can use Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) spray, which is safe. In Africa, many farmers use wood ash to dust potatoesâit reduces rot and insect damage. With strict sanitation and monitoring, you can keep storage losses below 10%.

lessons.title: Processing Potatoes: Chips, Fries, and Starch
lessons.body:
Processing turns potatoes into higher-value products. Chips, fries, and starch are the most common. Start with clean, mature potatoes. Wash them thoroughly to remove soil. Peel if desired (peeling reduces yield but improves texture). For chips (crisps), slice potatoes thinly (1â2 mm) using a mandoline or sharp knife. Soak slices in cold water for 30 minutes to remove excess starchâthis makes them crispy. Dry them with a clean cloth. Fry in vegetable oil at 170â180Â°C for 2â3 minutes until golden. Remove and drain on paper towels. Salt immediately. For fries, cut potatoes into 1 cm thick strips. Blanch in hot water (80Â°C) for 5 minutes, then dry. Fry at 160Â°C for 3 minutes, then increase to 180Â°C for 2 minutes until golden. For frozen fries, blanch, dry, and freeze on trays before packing.

For starch, grate or blend raw potatoes with water. Strain through a fine cloth or sieve. Let the liquid settle for 4â6 hours. A white layer of starch forms at the bottom. Pour off water, add fresh water, stir, and settle again. Repeat 2â3 times until water is clear. Spread the starch on a tray and dry in the sun or a low oven (50Â°C). Break into powder. Store in airtight containers. About 10 kg of potatoes yields 1â1.5 kg of starch.

In Africa, processing can be done at home or in small workshops. Use a grater, blender, or even a clean cement block to crush potatoes. For frying, use a deep pan or a local fryer. Maintain oil temperature with a thermometer. Change oil regularlyâold oil makes dark, unhealthy products. Package chips and fries in airtight bags or containers. Label with date. Starch can be used in baking, as a thickener, or sold to industries. With simple equipment, you can add value and earn more from your potato harvest.

lessons.title: Value-Added Potato Products
lessons.body:
Value-added products let you sell potatoes at a higher price and reduce waste. Beyond chips and fries, you can make potato flour, crisps, mashed potato powder, and even animal feed. Potato flour is made by drying peeled, sliced potatoes and grinding them into powder. Use a solar dryer or sun-dry on racks for 2â3 days until brittle. Grind in a mill. Potato flour is gluten-free and can be mixed with wheat flour for baking. It sells for 2â3 times the price of fresh potatoes.

Mashed potato powder: Cook potatoes, mash them, and dry the mash on trays at 60Â°C until completely dry. Grind into powder. To use, add hot water and milk. This is convenient for hotels and schools. Crisps (chips) can be flavoured with local spices like chili, paprika, or salt and vinegar. Package in small sachets for sale. Frozen fries are in high demand in citiesâblanch, fry lightly, freeze, and pack. You need a freezer, but you can rent space in a cold room.

Animal feed: Small or damaged potatoes can be boiled and mixed with bran or maize to feed pigs and chickens. Never feed raw green potatoesâthey are toxic. Cook them well. This reduces waste and feeds your livestock.

To succeed, focus on quality and hygiene. Use clean equipment, wear gloves, and package attractively. Label your products with a name and date. Sell to local shops, schools, restaurants, and markets. Start smallâtest the market with 5 kg of chips. Calculate your costs: 1 kg of fresh potatoes costs about $0.50, and 1 kg of chips sells for $5â10. With consistent quality, you can build a brand. In Africa, potato processing is a growing business. Join a cooperative or train others to increase volume. Always keep records of your costs and sales to know your profit.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Storage and Processing of Potatoes in Africa

This reference distils the operational essentials from the six lessons in the Storage and Processing module. It is written for the working potato grower, trader, or small processor who needs numbers, not theory. Every figure is drawn from published research or official extension guidance, and every recommendation is framed around one question: does it protect or increase the value of the crop?

Potato is a perishable, high-moisture crop â typically 75â80% water â and in sub-Saharan Africa post-harvest losses of 20â40% are common where storage and handling are poor. In Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, and Ethiopia, potatoes are among the top food-security crops, yet the gap between farm-gate price at harvest and off-season price can be two to three times. That gap is the business opportunity. Storage, grading, and processing are the tools that capture it.

Storage fundamentals at a glance

Potato tubers are living tissue. After harvest they respire, transpire, and, if wounded, heal. Storage is simply the management of three variables â temperature, humidity, and air movement â to slow respiration and prevent disease. The optimum for table potatoes is 4â8Â°C with 90â95% relative humidity; for processing potatoes destined for chips or fries, 7â10Â°C is preferred to limit reducing-sugar accumulation that causes dark fry colour. In most of tropical Africa, ambient temperatures of 18â30Â°C mean that without ventilation, evaporative cooling, or refrigeration, storage life is measured in weeks, not months.

The single most cost-effective intervention for smallholders is a well-ventilated, shaded, raised-floor store â often called a diffused-light store or improved ventilated store. Diffused-light storage keeps tubers in light bright enough to suppress sprouting but not so bright that greening (chlorophyll and solanine accumulation) becomes a problem. This is a proven, low-cost technology used across Kenya, Ethiopia, and Rwanda.

Design and ventilation principles

A functional store does four jobs: keeps rain and sun off the crop, moves air through the pile, excludes rodents and insects, and allows inspection. The raised-floor design â tubers on slatted pallets or in crates 30â40 cm off the ground â is essential in humid climates. Air must move through the gaps, not just over the top. A ridge vent or chimney at the highest point lets warm, moist air escape, while low-level inlets draw in cooler night air. In the diagram above, the two inlet arrows and the chimney create a stack effect: as warm air rises, it is replaced by cooler air from below.

For larger operations, forced-air ventilation with a thermostat-controlled fan is standard. The rule of thumb from commercial storage engineering is 0.05â0.1 mÂ³ of air per second per tonne of potatoes during the curing phase, dropping to 0.02â0.04 mÂ³/s/t during long-term holding. Over-ventilation dries and shrivels tubers; under-ventilation causes heat build-up and condensation, which drives soft rot.

Table 1: Storage conditions by end use

End use Temperature Relative humidity Expected storage life Key risk
Table / fresh market4â8Â°C90â95%3â6 monthsSprouting, greening
Processing (chips/fries)7â10Â°C90â95%4â8 monthsReducing sugars â dark fry
Seed potatoes2â4Â°C90â95%6â9 monthsPremature sprouting, virus
Diffused-light (tropical, no cooling)15â25Â°C70â85%2â4 monthsWeight loss, greening
Ambient tropical (uncontrolled)20â30Â°CVariable2â6 weeksRot, sprouting, shrinkage

Source: FAO, Post-harvest Losses in Potatoes (2018); CIP, Potato Storage and Post-Harvest Management (2019); KARLO/National Potato Council of Kenya extension materials.

Managing temperature and humidity

Curing is the first step and is often skipped. After harvest, hold tubers at 15â20Â°C and 85â90% RH for 10â14 days. This heals cuts and thickens the skin, reducing subsequent rot. Then cool gradually â no faster than 0.5Â°C per day â to the target holding temperature. Rapid cooling causes condensation and black spot.

Humidity control in tropical stores is mostly about preventing condensation, not adding moisture. The danger point is when warm daytime air cools at night and water condenses on tubers. Good insulation under the roof and continuous ventilation at dusk reduce this. A simple sling psychrometer or a cheap digital thermo-hygrometer (US$10â20) is a worthwhile investment; record readings twice daily.

Disease and pest control in storage

The main storage diseases are bacterial soft rot (Pectobacterium spp.), dry rot (Fusarium spp.), late blight (Phytophthora infestans), and silver scurf. The main pests are potato tuber moth (Phthorimaea operculella), which is severe in warm, unrefrigerated stores across Africa, and rodents. The most effective controls are cultural: harvest in dry weather, avoid bruising, cure properly, remove diseased tubers before storage, and keep the store clean between seasons. Tuber moth can be managed with diffused-light storage, pheromone traps, and the biological control Bacillus thuringiensis; chemical fumigants are rarely justified for smallholders and carry residue and safety risks.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Fumigation and chemical treatment of stored potatoes

Fumigants such as phosphine and chloropicrin are highly toxic. They must only be applied by trained, licensed operators using approved respiratory protection, in sealed stores, with clear warning signage and a mandatory re-entry interval. Never enter a fumigated store without self-contained breathing apparatus. In many African countries, on-farm fumigation is restricted or prohibited; check with your national plant protection authority. For smallholder stores, use non-chemical methods â diffused light, pheromone traps, Bt, and strict sanitation â instead.

Processing: chips, fries, and starch

Processing turns a bulky, perishable tuber into a storable, higher-margin product. The three main value chains are crisps (chips), French fries, and starch. For crisps and fries, the critical quality parameter is reducing sugar content: below 0.1% fresh weight gives light golden colour; above 0.3% gives dark, bitter product and elevated acrylamide. This is why storage temperature for processing potatoes must stay at 7â10Â°C, and why reconditioning (holding at 15â18Â°C for 2â3 weeks before frying) is used to lower sugars.

For starch, the process is simpler and less quality-sensitive: wash, grind, extract, settle, dry. Small-scale starch production can be profitable where there is a market for food-grade or industrial starch, but margins are thin and water use is high. In Africa, the strongest small-processor opportunities are crisps and frozen fries for urban markets, and dried potato products (flour, flakes, dried chips) for institutional buyers and off-season supply.

Table 2: Indicative economics of small-scale potato processing (per 100 kg fresh tubers)

Product Yield Key inputs Indicative farm-gate value uplift Main market
Fresh graded tubers95 kgGrading, packaging1.0Ã (baseline)Urban fresh markets
Crisps (chips)25â30 kgOil, salt, packaging, labour2.5â4ÃRetail, kiosks, schools
Frozen French fries45â55 kgBlanching, freezing, packaging2â3ÃRestaurants, supermarkets
Dried potato chips/flakes20â25 kgDrying fuel, milling1.5â2.5ÃInstitutional, off-season
Starch12â18 kgWater, settling, drying1.5â2ÃFood and industrial

Source: Compiled from FAO, Small-scale Potato Processing (2016); CIP, Value Addition in Potato (2020); and East African processor case studies (Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda). Values are indicative and vary with oil price, labour cost, and market access.

Value-added products and business logic

The business case for processing rests on three advantages: price stability, reduced waste, and market access. A grower who sells only fresh tubers at harvest is a price-taker. A grower who stores for three months and sells graded potatoes, or who processes into crisps, captures the off-season premium and the processing margin. In Kenya, the National Potato Council and CIP have supported small processor groups producing crisps and fries for supermarkets and schools. In Rwanda and Uganda, dried potato products and flour are growing segments.

Start small. A single fryer, a hand slicer, a solar dryer, and good packaging can be enough to test a market. Reinvest profits into cold storage or a larger dryer. Track three numbers weekly: cost per kg of raw tubers, yield per kg of product, and selling price per kg. If the margin is under 30%, fix the process before scaling.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Harvest dry, handle gently. Bruising is the entry point for most storage rots.
  2. Cure for 10â14 days at 15â20Â°C and 85â90% RH before cooling.
  3. Cool slowly â no more than 0.5Â°C per day â to 4â8Â°C (table) or 7â10Â°C (processing).
  4. Ventilate continuously with raised floors and a ridge vent; avoid condensation at dusk.
  5. Inspect weekly and remove diseased or sprouting tubers immediately.
  6. Never mix seed, table, and processing potatoes in the same store.
  7. For processing, test reducing sugars before frying; recondition at 15â18Â°C if needed.
  8. Keep records of temperature, humidity, weight loss, and margins â data drives better decisions.

Further Reading (free official sources)

  • FAO â Post-harvest Losses in Potatoes (2018)
  • International Potato Center (CIP) â Postharvest and Storage Resources
  • CTA â Potato Storage Extension Guide
  • National Potato Council of Kenya â Grower and Processor Resources
  • IITA â Root and Tuber Postharvest Technologies

quiz.q: What is the ideal storage temperature for table potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Table potatoes store best at 4â7Â°C to slow respiration without causing chilling injury.

quiz.q: Why should potatoes be cured before storage?
options: B) To heal cuts and thicken skin
C) To make them sprout faster
quiz.explanation: Curing heals wounds and thickens the skin, reducing rot and weight loss during storage.

quiz.q: What is the recommended relative humidity for storing table potatoes?
quiz.explanation: 90â95% relative humidity prevents shrivelling and weight loss.

quiz.q: Which material is best for storing small quantities of potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Jute sacks allow ventilation and help regulate humidity, unlike airtight plastic.

quiz.q: How often should stored potatoes be inspected?
quiz.explanation: Regular inspection every two weeks helps remove rotting tubers before they spread disease.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of ventilation in a potato store?
options: B) To remove heat and moisture
quiz.explanation: Ventilation removes excess heat and moisture, preventing rot and sprouting.

quiz.q: In a raised slatted store, how high should the floor be above ground?
quiz.explanation: A floor at least 30 cm above ground prevents moisture and rodent entry.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to cool potatoes in dry areas?
quiz.explanation: An evaporative charcoal cooler uses wet charcoal to lower temperature by 5â10Â°C.

quiz.q: What happens if potatoes are stored below 4Â°C?
options: B) They become sweet and develop chilling injury
quiz.explanation: Temperatures below 4Â°C cause chilling injury and convert starch to sugar, making them sweet.

quiz.q: How can you increase humidity in a potato store?
options: B) Place pans of water on the floor
quiz.explanation: Shallow pans of water or wetting the floor raises humidity without wetting the potatoes directly.

quiz.q: Which disease causes brown, greasy patches and a foul smell in stored potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Late blight causes brown, greasy lesions and a distinctive foul odour.

quiz.q: What is a safe method to control potato tuber moth?
quiz.explanation: Pheromone traps attract and kill male moths, reducing infestation.

quiz.q: Why should you never mix old and new potatoes in storage?
options: B) Old potatoes can infect new ones with disease
C) New potatoes need more humidity
quiz.explanation: Old potatoes may carry diseases that spread to the new crop.

quiz.q: What is the recommended bleach solution for cleaning a potato store?
options: A) 1 part bleach to 1 part water
B) 1 part bleach to 10 parts water
C) 1 part bleach to 100 parts water
quiz.explanation: A 1:10 bleach solution disinfects surfaces without being too harsh.

quiz.q: What is the first step in making potato chips (crisps)?
options: B) Soak slices in cold water
quiz.explanation: Soaking slices in cold water removes excess starch, making chips crispier.

quiz.q: At what temperature should you fry potato chips?
quiz.explanation: 170â180Â°C is ideal for golden, crispy chips without burning.

quiz.q: How much starch can you get from 10 kg of potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Potatoes yield about 10â15% starch by weight, so 10 kg gives 1â1.5 kg.

quiz.q: What should you do after blanching fries before freezing?
quiz.explanation: Drying removes surface moisture, preventing ice crystals and oil splatter during frying.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of making potato flour?
options: B) It is cheaper than fresh potatoes
quiz.explanation: Potato flour is gluten-free, making it valuable for people with gluten intolerance.

quiz.q: How should you dry mashed potato for powder?
options: A) In direct sun for 1 hour
quiz.explanation: Drying at 60Â°C removes moisture without cooking or burning the mash.

quiz.q: Why should you never feed raw green potatoes to animals?
quiz.explanation: Green potatoes contain solanine, which is toxic to animals and humans.

quiz.q: What is a good packaging material for homemade crisps?
quiz.explanation: Airtight packaging keeps crisps crunchy and prevents moisture absorption.

quiz.q: What should you label on packaged potato products?
quiz.explanation: Labelling with name and date ensures traceability and builds trust.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to add value to small or damaged potatoes?
options: B) Boil and feed to livestock
quiz.explanation: Boiling damaged potatoes and mixing with bran makes safe, nutritious animal feed.

quiz.q: What is the approximate profit margin for 1 kg of chips if potatoes cost $0.50/kg and chips sell for $5/kg?
quiz.explanation: Profit is selling price minus cost: $5.00 - $0.50 = $4.50 per kg.

quiz.q: Why is record-keeping important in potato processing?
options: A) To know your profit and costs
quiz.explanation: Records of costs and sales help you calculate profit and make better business decisions.

quiz.q: What is a common traditional storage method in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Pit or clamp storage is a traditional, low-cost method used in many African regions.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended stack height for stored potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Stacking no higher than 1.5 m prevents crushing and allows air circulation.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to measure humidity?
quiz.explanation: A hygrometer measures relative humidity in the storage environment.

quiz.q: What is the first step in processing potatoes into starch?
options: B) Grate or blend with water
quiz.explanation: Grating or blending releases starch granules, which are then washed and settled.
